newsitem.title: GERMANY: G7 welcomes dollar gains, says stability needed now.
newsitem.headline: G7 welcomes dollar gains, says stability needed now.

text.p: The world's financial leaders said on Saturday that they were satisfied with a bounce back in the U.S. dollar from the record lows hit two years ago but went out of their way to avoid giving the currency any new direction.
The so-called Group of Seven industrial nations said in a brief four-sentence statement that they believed the plunge in the dollar seen in spring of 1995 had now been corrected.
"We discussed the developments on currency and financial markets," said the statement, issued at the end of a one-day meeting in the German capital of Berlin.
"We believe that major misalignments in exchange markets, noted in our April 1995 communique, have been corrected.

"We reaffirmed our views that exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals and that excess volatility is undesirable. We agreed to monitor developments on the currency markets and to coooperate as appropriate," it continued.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who chaired the meeting, stressed that the agreement had been approved by all parties. "These are three sentences. They are clear," he said.

The Group of Seven officials came to Berlin facing the dilemma of how to at once welcome the currency' recovery from 1995 lows, which the G7 itself fostered, without sending a signal to markets that could prompt a further surge or slide.

In a bid to find their way out of this dilemma, the top officials from Germany, Britain, Canada, France, Italy, Japan and the United States opted to stress that they were comfortable with the dollar's recent gains.
But they also made absolutely clear that what was now needed was for currencies to remain stable at current levels.
Although there were no explicit threats made, it was clear that any volatility could be countered by central banks' intervening in the market to influence currency rates.

The question of the dollar's strength had been expected to dominate the meeting, held in the Kronprinzenpalais, the historic building in which the treaty joining the two halves of Germany was signed in 1990.

The dollar's surge of more than seven percent since the start of the year, seen by some G7 members as potentially destabilising because of the speed of the change, put currency rates firmly on the top of the agenda before the talks.

The dollar, which added a further two pfennigs on Friday to trade above 1.67 marks, eased to close at aound 1.6630 marks late Friday after the United States signalled that it believed that its currency could now stabilise.
The G7's agenda also covered a wide range of themes including the world economic outlook, Europe's single currency plans, debt relief for poor nations and increased bank surveillance.
Waigel said that the G7 had exchanged views on the global economy, agreeing that low inflation and low interest rates created good conditions for sustained growth.
They had also discussed the way forward on increased debt relief for poor nations would be addressed in more detail later this year, he added.

In a brief discussion on Europe's plans to create a single currency, the four European partners in the seven-nation bloc had assured their counterparts that the new currency would be stable and would be launched on time in 1999, Waigel said.
